## What it is

Gelman named the effect while answering a reader, Seth, who nominated a map of telephone calls between U.S. locations as his "candidate for bad graphic of the year" because he "learned nothing" from it. Gelman agreed at first, then defended the graph: it "has the pleasant feature of revealing things we already knew", for example that "Minneapolis, Chicago, and Detroit are in the upper midwest, whereas Boston, New York, and Philadelphia are tightly packed in the northeast." He continues: "I call this the Chris Rock effect. Chris Rock says things we all know are true. But he says it so well that we get a shock of recognition, the joy of relearning what we already know, but hearing it in a new way that makes us think more deeply about all sorts of related topics."

Some statistical graphics work the same way. They show a pattern you already knew existed so vividly that you start asking questions you hadn't thought to ask. The simulation below uses our own example, births by day of the year, rather than Gelman's map.

## Why it matters

We often judge graphs by whether they reveal something *new*. Gelman points out that confirming the known has value too. It builds trust in the data, since if the familiar patterns show up the data are probably sound. It provides a reference frame for the surprising parts, and it invites deeper thinking. A graph that shows nothing you already knew is often a sign that something is wrong with the data or the display.

## How it works

The effect needs a display that preserves enough detail for the familiar patterns to stand out against the noise. For daily data, that might mean showing every day of the year rather than monthly averages, or separating the weekly cycle from the seasonal one. When the known patterns appear crisply, the reader trusts the graph and turns to the residual surprises.

## Simulated example

Simulated daily births over a year, built with a weekday/weekend cycle, a gentle seasonal wave and dips on major holidays. The raw series looks like noisy zigzags. Switch to "Day of year, averaged over weekdays" to get the moment of recognition.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, mean, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof view = Inputs.radio(["Raw daily series", "Day of year, averaged over weekdays"], {value: "Raw daily series", label: "Display"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 42, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
births = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const holidays = {1: "New Year", 185: "July 4", 359: "Christmas", 327: "Thanksgiving*", 245: "Labor Day*", 304: "Halloween"};
  const years = [2001, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005];
  return years.flatMap((yr, k) => range(365).map(doy => {
    const dow = (doy + k) % 7;                          // shifts each year
    const weekend = dow >= 5 ? -0.22 : 0;
    const season = 0.05 * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * (doy - 100) / 365);
    const hol = holidays[doy + 1] ? (doy + 1 === 304 ? -0.05 : -0.3) : 0;
    const near = (holidays[doy] || holidays[doy + 2]) && !holidays[doy + 1] ? -0.06 : 0;
    return {yr, doy: doy + 1, dow, weekend: dow >= 5, births: 10000 * Math.exp(weekend + season + hol + near + r.normal(0, 0.025)), label: holidays[doy + 1]};
  }));
}
avgDoy = range(365).map(d => {
  const pts = births.filter(b => b.doy === d + 1 && !b.weekend);
  return {doy: d + 1, births: pts.length ? mean(pts.map(p => p.births)) : NaN, label: births.find(b => b.doy === d + 1).label};
}).filter(d => Number.isFinite(d.births))
```

```{ojs}
view === "Raw daily series"
  ? Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "The Chris Rock Effect: chart 1 of 2",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Day (5 years). Vertical axis: Births. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",height: 280, x: {label: "Day (5 years)"}, y: {label: "Births", grid: true},
      marks: [Plot.line(births.map((d, i) => ({...d, i})), {x: "i", y: "births", stroke: "#2166ac", strokeWidth: 0.5})]})
  : Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "The Chris Rock Effect: chart 2 of 2",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Day of year. Vertical axis: Average weekday births. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",height: 300, x: {label: "Day of year"}, y: {label: "Average weekday births", grid: true},
      marks: [
        Plot.line(avgDoy, {x: "doy", y: "births", stroke: "#2166ac"}),
        Plot.text(avgDoy.filter(d => d.label), {x: "doy", y: "births", text: "label", dy: 12, fill: "#d6604d", fontSize: 10})
      ]})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`${view === "Raw daily series" ? "The raw series is a blur of weekly zigzags. Switch displays." : "There it is: the holiday dips and the seasonal wave. You knew all of this, and now you *see* it, and the next question is about the dips on the days next to each holiday."} (Holidays marked * are placed at a fixed day for simplicity.)`}</div>`
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Graphs that show familiar patterns well build trust and prompt new questions.
- If a graph shows none of the patterns you know should be there, suspect the data or the display.
- Choose displays that separate known structure (cycles, seasons) so the surprises stand out.
:::
